title: Dyer v. MacDougall
lead: A defamation plaintiff offers no admissible account that the two challenged statements occurred. After declining additional depositions, he seeks a trial in the hope that the witnesses’ demeanor or questioning will reverse their uniform denials.

actors.name: Dyer
actors.role: Defamation plaintiff connected with Queensboro Corporation.

actors.name: Albert E. MacDougall and his wife
actors.role: Alleged speakers who denied making the statements.

actors.name: Almirall
actors.role: Lawyer alleged to have heard one statement; denied it by affidavit.

actors.name: Dorothy Russell Hope
actors.role: Dyer’s sister-in-law and alleged hearer of the other statement; denied it in a deposition.

proceedings: The district court entered dismissal of counts three and four on January 7, 1952, leaving two other counts pending.
On March 4 it supplied the Rule 54(b) determination; Dyer appealed that day.
The Second Circuit held the appeal timely and affirmed the two-count dismissal on December 31, 1952; Frank separately concurred.
limits: This source-brief account states historical Rule 54(b) and evidentiary rules, without a new audit or current-rules claim. Only counts three and four were decided. Hope’s account was a deposition, not an affidavit. Frank agreed with the result but rejected Hand’s general appellate-review rationale.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: Dyer alleges separate defamatory statements connected to his corporate dealings
sections.cue: Which two accusations became the subject of this appeal?
paragraphs: Dyer’s amended complaint contained four counts arising from his dealings with Queensboro Corporation. Count three alleged that Albert E. MacDougall told lawyer Almirall that Dyer’s shareholder letter was a blackmailing letter. Count four alleged that MacDougall’s wife, as his agent, made a similar statement to Dorothy Russell Hope, the sister of Dyer’s wife. Other counts involved a directors’ meeting statement and a written letter.

The challenged conversations occurred outside Dyer’s presence. Both MacDougalls and Almirall supplied affidavits, and Hope gave a deposition Dyer had taken. Each alleged speaker denied speaking and each alleged hearer denied hearing. Dyer’s affidavits offered no admissible affirmative proof of either utterance.

sections.title: The district court offers discovery before dismissing two counts
sections.cue: Why was the later appeal timely despite the January judgment?
paragraphs: Defendants initially moved before answering against counts two, three and four, then withdrew as to two. The judge offered depositions of both MacDougalls and Almirall and another of Hope. By consent the hearing was adjourned for discovery. After several months Dyer declined those examinations, maintaining that courtroom questioning might expose false denials or yield admissions.

In December 1951 the judge found no trial-worthy issue on counts three and four, and judgment entered January 7, 1952. Dyer did not appeal within thirty days and later sought extension and reargument. On March 4 the judge adhered to dismissal but expressly directed judgment and found no reason for delay. Dyer appealed that day.

The Second Circuit denied defendants’ motion to dismiss the appeal. Under then-current Rule 54(b), the partial multiple-claim disposition became appealable only with that determination. Each utterance was a distinct wrong by words, occasion or speaker; a common employment connection did not fuse the claims. Two counts remained pending, so March 4 was the first appealable day. This did not establish a general power to revive every untimely appeal.

sections.title: Hand finds no admissible account filling the evidentiary gap
sections.cue: What happened to Dyer’s proposed hearsay chain?
paragraphs: Judge Learned Hand wrote the principal opinion for a panel with Chief Judge Swan and Judge Frank. Defendants bore the motion burden, but Dyer would have to prove the utterances at trial. Showing that his proof could not reach a jury justified summary judgment. Because he declined discovery, the court assumed the witnesses would repeat their existing denials, separately considering the possibility of new admissions.

Dyer said his wife reported that Hope said she could forgive him everything except the shareholder letter. No affidavit from his wife was supplied, but even assuming one, Hope’s alleged declaration was hearsay. The alleged defamatory call was not sufficiently timed to support spontaneous exclamation; even a presumed one-day interval did not show speech under continuing sudden emotional stress.

Calling Hope himself would not make the wife’s contrary version admissible under the historical rules considered. Rule 43(b)’s adverse-party provision did not cover nonparty Hope. Thus the proposed chain supplied no substantive evidence of the slanders and did not overcome uniform denials.

sections.title: Demeanor might be evidence, but Hand rejects a merely theoretical hope of success
sections.cue: Why did further admissions require a demonstrated reason to expect them?
paragraphs: Hand acknowledged that hesitation, discomfort, arrogance or defiance could suggest a fabricated denial and sometimes imply the opposite fact. He did not deem demeanor universally uninformative or denials automatically truthful.

Nevertheless, allowing this claim to reach a jury solely through a theoretical demeanor impression would make a directed-verdict ruling depend on impressions unavailable in a printed appellate record. He preferred effective appellate review over the exceedingly rare possibility that demeanor alone rationally supplied a case. He distinguished the equivalent of directing a verdict from the potentially broader power to set a verdict aside.

Live questioning might also yield additional substantive admissions, a different possibility. Deposition evasiveness or recalcitrance could support expecting more testimony in a judge’s presence. Dyer had refused those depositions and thus supplied no concrete basis for that expectation. The court would not presume it in the abstract.

sections.title: Frank affirms only on the unusual facts
sections.cue: What part of Hand’s explanation did he reject?
paragraphs: Judge Frank objected that Hand’s approach could allow a nonjury judge to rely on demeanor while denying a jury the same evidence, making summary judgment depend on requesting a jury. He also thought appellate-review concerns overstated: both trial and appellate judges assessing directed verdicts assume evidence and reasonable inferences favor the opponent, without relying on the trial judge’s personal credibility view. New-trial motions, where judges can weigh credibility, are different.

Frank rejected an invariant rule barring a plaintiff whenever the only available witness denies the allegation despite demeanor thoroughly persuading the factfinder of falsity. Such a rule could cause serious injustice. He nonetheless affirmed on this peculiar record: Dyer was absent, knew every available witness denied the statements, and had no independent account. In Frank’s view, the suit itself publicized the alleged slander, and disbelief of all adverse witnesses could not alone justify this trial.

On December 31, 1952, all three judges affirmed dismissal of counts three and four. Frank’s separate concurrence supported that limited result, not Hand’s general reasoning; there was no dissent. The two remaining defamation counts were unaffected.

sources.pinpoint: Frank concurrence; Holding and judgment; 201 F.2d 269–272 & concurrence nn.1–9
